title: Godly Sorrow and the Comfort of Titus
summary: Paul calls the Corinthians to cleanse themselves and to make room for him in their hearts. He then resumes the story broken off in chapter 2: in Macedonia, pressed by conflicts and fears, he was comforted by the arrival of Titus and his news that the church had responded to Paul's severe letter with grief, zeal, and repentance. Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which leads to repentance and salvation, from worldly sorrow, which brings death, and rejoices in his complete confidence in them.
story: At 2:13 Paul left Troas for Macedonia, restless because Titus had not come. Then he turned aside into a long reflection on the ministry of the new covenant (2:14-7:4). Here, at 7:5, the story picks up again with Paul in Macedonia, and the news finally arrives. It is good news: the relationship broken by the painful visit and the tearful letter is being restored. This chapter closes the first major section of the letter (chapters 1-7) on a note of joy and confidence, which prepares the ground for the request about the collection for Jerusalem in chapters 8 and 9.
historical:
Paul had written a severe letter, delivered or followed up by Titus, calling the Corinthians to deal with a man who had wronged someone (verse 12; compare 2:5-11). He waited anxiously for the outcome, first at Troas and then in Macedonia, the northern Greek region whose churches included Philippi and Thessalonica. His phrase "our bodies had no rest" and his reference to "conflicts on the outside, fears within" suggest continued opposition in Macedonia as well as inner anxiety about Corinth.

Verse 12 speaks of "the one who did wrong" and "the one who was harmed". Some take the injured party to be Paul himself, insulted during his painful visit; others think of another member of the church. Those who identify the offender with the incestuous man of 1 Corinthians 5 sometimes suggest the one harmed was his father, but that identification is less common today. Paul's point is that the letter's real aim was not settling one case but showing the church its own devotion.
cultural:
Ancient letters were carried by trusted messengers, who often delivered news and explanations in person along with the written text and then brought back a report. Titus played exactly that role, and his personal account of the Corinthians' longing, mourning, and zeal mattered to Paul as much as any written reply. The emotional vocabulary of the chapter, longing, mourning, indignation, alarm, zeal, reflects the way honor and shame shaped relationships in the Greek and Roman world; the Corinthians' eagerness to clear themselves (verse 11) was a public restoring of honor between them and their founder.

The phrase "with fear and trembling" in verse 15 was a common biblical expression for humble respect, not terror (compare Philippians 2:12; Ephesians 6:5). The Corinthians received Titus as Paul's representative with proper seriousness.
literary: Verse 1 concludes the passage begun at 6:14, drawing out the consequence of the promises just quoted. Verses 2-4 return to the personal appeal of 6:11-13 ("Make room for us in your hearts"), with three short denials of wrongdoing and a burst of confidence. Verses 5-16 are narrative and reflection, bound together by repeated words: comfort (paraklesis and its verb appear seven times), sorrow (which runs through verses 8-11), joy, and confidence. Verse 11 is a rhetorical cascade, seven exclamations beginning "what", spilling out the effects of godly sorrow. The chapter closes where it began, in confidence: "I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you."

outline.t: Perfecting holiness in the fear of God
Make room for us in your hearts
Godly sorrow that leads to repentance

doctrines.note: Verse 10 gives one of the Bible's clearest descriptions of repentance: "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death." Worldly sorrow is regret over consequences or exposure, and it leads to despair; godly sorrow turns toward God and leads to change and life.

Verse 1 calls believers to "cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit". Holiness is both a gift (God's promises) and a pursuit (perfecting it), and it touches the whole person, outward conduct and inner life alike.

"God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus" (verse 6). God's comfort came through an ordinary event: a friend arriving with good news. Paul sees God's hand in the timing and the people of his life.

words.note: Metanoia, repentance, literally a change of mind, but in the New Testament a turning of the whole person, mind, will, and life, away from sin and toward God. Paul uses it rarely (also Romans 2:4). Here it is the fruit of sorrow rightly directed, and it leads to salvation.

Paraklesis, encouragement or comfort, from a verb meaning to call alongside. The word dominates 2 Corinthians (it opens the letter in 1:3-7) and this chapter. Comfort in Paul is not merely soothing; it is strength given by someone who comes alongside, whether God or a friend like Titus.

Ametameletos, without regret, not to be regretted. In verse 10 it describes the repentance that leads to salvation: a sorrow no one looks back on with regret. The same word describes God's gifts and calling in Romans 11:29, which are irrevocable.

christ: Christ is not named in this chapter, but its movement is shaped by the gospel. The promises that ground the call to holiness in verse 1 are the promises of God fulfilled in Christ, in whom they are all "Yes" (1:20). Godly sorrow leads to salvation because Christ's death has made forgiveness possible; repentance is a turning toward the God who reconciled the world to himself in Christ (5:19). And the pattern of the chapter, grief followed by comfort, sorrow turned to joy, echoes the pattern Paul has traced in his own sufferings, the death of Jesus carried in the body so that his life may be revealed (4:10). Where the connection is thematic rather than stated, it is still the logic of the whole letter.

hard.q: How can Paul say he does not regret causing the Corinthians sorrow, and how does someone tell godly sorrow from the kind that brings death?
hard.a:
Paul admits he did regret the letter for a time (verse 8), which is an honest picture of pastoral pain. He does not rejoice that they were hurt; he rejoices that the hurt led to repentance. A doctor who sets a broken bone causes pain without regretting the treatment. Paul's claim is not that inflicting pain is good but that truth told in love can wound in order to heal.

The difference between the two sorrows lies in where they turn. Godly sorrow turns toward God, admits wrong, receives forgiveness, and produces change (the earnestness and zeal of verse 11). Worldly sorrow turns inward: it can be shame, self-hatred, or despair that does not believe forgiveness is possible, and it ends in death. For a reader caught in sorrow that feels like the second kind, the gospel's answer is that God "comforts the downcast" (verse 6), often through people. Speaking to a trusted pastor, friend, or counselor, and seeking professional help when sorrow becomes crushing, is one of the ways that comfort arrives.

questions: Think of a time you were sorry for something. Was it sorrow over what you had done, or over being found out? What was the difference in what followed?
God comforted Paul through the arrival of Titus. Who has God used to comfort you, and whom might you comfort this week?
Paul risked the relationship by writing a hard letter, and it was restored. When is it loving to say something that will cause pain?
